newsitem.title: CHINA: China yuan interbank market stabilises after falls.
newsitem.headline: China yuan interbank market stabilises after falls.

text.p: Interest rates on the renminbi interbank market in China are expected to move in a narrow range in the next few weeks following sharp falls in the wake of last month's bank interest rate cut, traders said on Thursday.

The rates, calculated on an annual basis, are now mainly moving in a range of between 11.00 and 12.00 percent against 12.00 to 13.00 percent before the falls and the trend is unlikely to change in the short term, they said.
The People's Bank of China cut interest rates for bank deposits and loans respectively by an average of 1.5 and 1.2 percentage points on August 23.

"Lenders and borrowers have struck a new balance after the falls," said one trader. "In the next few weeks, the rates are likely to consolidate at the present levels if there is no market-moving news."
"There has been no fresh stimulus since the bank interest rate cut," said a second trader.
"Trading has been dull for the past two weeks. The trend is likely to continue in the short term," he added.
The most important factor in the mid-term will be a possible cut in the bank reserve ratio, traders said. In early July, the central bank promised such a cut before the end of this year.

Chinese commercial banks and other financial institutions must put aside 13 percent of their deposits as reserves for the central bank and another five to seven percent for themselves, both deposited in the central bank.
Traders said large funds were expected to be released if there was such a cut and would break the cash balance on the interbank market again.
"We expect the rates to fall by one percentage point on average after the bank reserve ratio cut," said one trader. "This means the rates will move in a range of 10.00 to 11.00 percent."
Traders said the market rates would come under further downward pressure in the long term with China's national economy improving and inflation falling steadily.

Official figures issued on Wednesday said China's retail price inflation was a year-on-year 6.8 percent in the first eight months of this year, compared with a year-on-year 14.8 percent for all of 1995.
China is reducing an anti-infaltionary subsidy for long-term treasury bonds and deposits of three years and above. Traders expect the subsidy to be scrapped by the end of this year.
